Arctic sea ice hit its peak on March 22, 2025 at 5.53 million square miles (14.33 million square kilometers), making it the lowest annual peak on record. In the Antarctic, sea ice melts during the Southern Hemisphere summer to its annual minimum extent. This year, Antarctic sea ice retreated to 764,000 square miles (1.98 million square kilometers) on March 1, tying for the second lowest minimum extent ever recorded. The loss of ice in both polar regions has led to another milestone — the total amount of sea ice on Earth reached a new record low this year, according to NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration and the National Snow and Ice Data Center. Full story: https://go.nasa.gov/3XK3V7RNASA Climate Change897.4K views · April 3, 20251:21📍Mendenhall Glacier, southeast Alaska These #Landsat images show how the size of the Mendenhall Glacier changed from 1986 to 2024, using infrared bands to differentiate ice, rocks & soil, and vegetation. The glacier has retreated about a mile, and in some places thinned by 2,000 feet. Although Mendenhall’s retreat began centuries ago, warming have accelerated its decline. Between 2005 and 2019, the wider Juneau Icefield (Mendenhall’s source) lost 63 of 1,050 glaciers and 10% of its ice. Satellites like Landsat help scientists track these changes over time. #Alaska #Glacier #Ice #NASA #NASAEarthNASA Climate Change36.1K views · March 4, 20250:04More and more, mountain snow in the high-altitude region surrounding Mount Everest and the Himalayas is disappearing. Scientists measure and track the winter snow line – the elevation at and above which seasonal snow persists on top of glacial ice. Over time, this line has been creeping higher and higher in the region due to a combination of warmer and drier conditions. As a result, snow is becoming more sparse at lower elevations in the Himalayas and surrounding area. The change is visible in these Landsat 9 images from January 2022 and 2025. The shift has implications for water availability and fire activity. Low seasonal snowpack and snow persistence affect downstream communities’ water security, reducing supplies for agriculture and other needs. A prolonged winter drought has also contributed to an early start to the 2025 fire season in parts of Nepal. Full story: https://go.nasa.gov/41qxzkTNASA Climate Change485.3K views · February 20, 20250:082024 was the hottest year in NASA’s record, which starts in 1880. Global temperatures were around 1.28 degrees Celsius (2.30 degrees Fahrenheit) higher in 2024 than the 1951-1980 average, the baseline period used in GISTEMP. Full story: https://go.nasa.gov/40b8Xe7 Although there are slight variations from year to year and from region to region, overall, Earth has been experiencing a long-term warming trend. In fact, the past 10 years have been the warmest 10 on record. How are we sure that Earth is warming? Our partners at National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and other organizations worldwide keep their own separate records and use different calculation methods. Their records agree with NASA’s. We also know that Earth’s current warming is caused by emissions of greenhouse gases, such as carbon dioxide and methane, that trap heat from the Sun near Earth’s surface. Human activities like energy generation, transportation, industry, and agriculture emit greenhouse gases. How do we know it’s us? From space, we can see that warming is happening close to Earth’s surface, while the upper atmosphere is cooling. This specific pattern acts like a fingerprint pointing to warming caused by increased greenhouse gases in the atmosphere. We can look for fingerprints of other culprits too, like specific patterns of warming and change that would be expected if the warming were caused by volcanic eruptions or changes in ocean circulation. The clues don’t line up for those. It’s humans. Around the world, average temperatures this November were 1.31°C (or about 2.36°F) warmer than the long-term 1951-1980 average for November. The above-average temperatures continue a long-term warming trend driven by human activities. Besides November 2023, this November was much warmer than any other November going back to 1880 – further increasing the odds that 2024 will become the hottest year on record.NASA Climate Change339K views · December 10, 20240:11Andros, the largest island in the Bahamas, is changing in unexpected ways due to sea level rise. From 1985 through 2018, local tide gauges show that sea levels rose around 10 cm (4 inches). This is similar to the global rise in sea level NASA satellites have measured. Scientists expected this rise to alter the island’s shoreline. When they examined images of the island over the years, like this #Landsat image pair from 1986 and 2024, they found that the coastline had not receded as much as expected. Rather, they found major changes to the island’s inland marshes and mudflats on the western side. In their analysis, they ruled out hurricanes as a cause for the noticeable change, as those impacts were temporary. The pair of #Landsat images highlights the changes in the distribution of bacterial mats and channels in the shallow tidal zone of the Three Creeks area in the northern part of the island.
